title: Able to keep you (Jude 20–25)
hookLine: the letter ends in praise to the one able to keep you from falling
tomorrow: who actually wrote these letters, and does it change anything?

cards: A toddler takes her first wobbly steps across the kitchen, and behind her, an inch from her back, a parent's hands hover. She thinks she's doing it alone. She mostly is.
So who keeps you from falling when you can't keep yourself? The letter of Jude is stormy reading, full of warnings and hard pictures: clouds without water, wandering stars.
And then, in its last lines, the storm breaks into praise, and the praise answers that question.

teach.h: KEEP YOURSELVES IN THE LOVE OF GOD.
teach.b: First, Jude gives the readers their part: "building up yourselves on your most holy faith, praying in the Holy Ghost, Keep yourselves in the love of God." Keep yourselves.

teach.h: ABLE TO KEEP YOU FROM FALLING.
teach.b: Then the last lines lift: "Now unto him that is able to keep you from falling, and to present you faultless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy, To the only wise God our Saviour, be glory and majesty, dominion and power, both now and ever. Amen."
Notice the word keep, twice. The readers are told to keep themselves in God's love, and then told who is able to keep them. Their part is real, like the toddler's steps.
But the last word isn't theirs.
A burst of praise like this, giving glory to God, is called a doxology, and some churches use Jude's as a blessing to close worship.
So a stormy letter doesn't end on the storm. It ends on the hands.

how: Some services end with a doxology or a blessing, and some churches use Jude 24–25 as the closing words of worship.

s: Jude is a gentle letter all the way through

a doxology is a burst of praise giving glory to God
Jude's ends: be glory and majesty, dominion and power.
Jude says keeping yourself is entirely up to you
keep yourselves, it says, and then praises him that is able to keep you.

games.q: at the end of a service, the pastor raises a hand and says, now unto him that is able to keep you from falling. your friend whispers: why say that at the end?
o: it's a doxology: the service ends in praise, like Jude.
it's a warning to people who might leave the church.
it's a closing prayer only clergy are meant to say.
games.why: a stormy letter ends in glory given to God, and some churches borrow its last lines to close worship the same way.

practice: If you'd like, say Jude's closing words out loud, slowly, a phrase at a time: now unto him that is able to keep you from falling. Or listen to them in your mind and rest on the one word keep. Let the rest of the sit be quiet.

wordCard.voice: Doxology. A burst of praise giving glory to God, like the lines that close the letter of Jude.
